meta.titre: Biological Drawing: from specimen to labelled diagram
meta.sous_theme: Drawing, labelling and magnification of a specimen

sections.contenu_markdown:
Esther revises for the GCE Biology paper and meets a question that asks for a large labelled diagram of a small animal she has studied in class.
She knows the animal well, yet her first attempt is tiny, shaded with the pencil, and the labels cross each other, so marks that her knowledge should have earned are lost.
Drawing questions come back year after year because the examiner can see at once whether a candidate has observed carefully.
This course teaches the rules that earn marks and shows how to apply them to any specimen, from an insect to a mould.

items: A specimen is a single example of an organism, or of an organ, that is being studied.
The body of an insect is divided into three main regions called the head, the thorax and the abdomen.
There are 10 millimetres (mm) in 1 centimetre (cm), and a ruler is used to measure length.

sections.titre: Drawing, labelling and measuring a biological specimen
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a biological drawing is
A biological drawing is a clear record of the parts of a specimen and of how they are arranged. It is a scientific record, not a work of art. You draw what you can see, in correct proportion, and nothing else.

### Rules that earn marks

| Feature | What to do | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Write the name of the specimen above or below the drawing | The examiner knows what you drew |
| Size | Draw large and use most of the space given | Small drawings hide detail |
| Pencil | Use a sharp pencil and keep an eraser | Fine lines can be corrected |
| Lines | Use single, smooth, continuous lines | Sketchy or doubled lines look uncertain |
| Shading | Do not shade or colour | Shading hides the outline of structures |
| Proportion | Keep each part in the right size compared with the others | Accuracy is judged |
| Labels | Write each label horizontally at the end of a straight, ruled line that touches the part | The part named is clear |
| Label lines | They must not cross each other | Crossing lines cause confusion |

### Magnification
The magnification tells how many times larger or smaller the drawing is than the specimen:

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{size of the drawing}}{\text{actual size of the specimen}}$$

Both lengths must be in the same unit. A value greater than 1 means the drawing is enlarged, and a value less than 1 means it is reduced. The magnification is written beside the title, for example $\times 3$.

### Draw or describe
Many questions say 'draw or describe'. A description must be ordered: start with the general shape and the main regions, then give the parts of each region and their positions. A well-organised description of this kind earns marks for the same points as a drawing.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the specimen is an insect such as a grasshopper, a cockroach or a fly
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Draw and label three regions in order: the **head** with one pair of antennae, a pair of compound eyes and the mouthparts; the **thorax** carrying three pairs of jointed legs and the wings; and the segmented **abdomen** with small breathing openings called spiracles along its sides.
Legs and wings are always attached to the thorax, never to the abdomen. A dipteran fly, such as the housefly, has only one pair of wings, because its second pair is reduced to two small knob-shaped balancing organs called halteres.

variantes.nom: Vertebrates such as a lizard or a fish
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the specimen has a backbone and you are asked for its external features
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A lizard is drawn in three regions: head, body and a long tail. Label the eye, the nostril, the ear opening, the scaly skin and the four limbs whose toes end in claws.
A bony fish such as tilapia has a head, a trunk and a tail. Label the mouth, nostril, eye, operculum (gill cover), scales, lateral line and the fins: dorsal, pectoral, pelvic, anal and caudal.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question names an organism such as Amoeba or a mould that is studied with a microscope
variantes.contenu_markdown:
An Amoeba is a single cell with a changing shape. Label the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, food vacuoles, contractile vacuole and pseudopodia (the extensions used for movement and feeding).
A mould fungus is made of thread-like hyphae that together form a mycelium. Upright hyphae carry a round sporangium that contains many spores. Moulds have no chlorophyll and usually feed on dead or decaying organic matter.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Make a large labelled drawing of the external features of a grasshopper as seen from the side, and write the magnification beside the title.

The grasshopper measures 40 mm from head to tip of abdomen, and your drawing measures 12 cm in the same direction.

etapes.action: Read the question and list what it asks for.
etapes.justification: Each key word is a mark: 'large', 'labelled', 'external', 'side view', 'magnification'.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A large side view, external parts only, ruled labels, a title and the magnification.

etapes.action: Observe the specimen and plan the space.
etapes.justification: Looking first prevents errors of proportion, and leaving room on one side keeps the label lines from crossing.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three regions in order from front to back: head, thorax, abdomen. The drawing takes the centre of the page and the labels go to the sides.

etapes.action: Draw the outline lightly, then go over it with firm single lines.
etapes.justification: Light lines can be erased, and firm continuous lines are what the examiner wants to see. No shading is used.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Head with antenna and eye, thorax with three legs and the wings, segmented abdomen. The long hind leg is drawn larger than the others.

etapes.action: Add the labels with a ruler.
etapes.justification: Straight horizontal label lines that touch the part make the answer clear.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Antenna, compound eye, mouthparts, head, thorax, forewing, hind wing, foreleg, middle leg, hind leg, spiracle, tympanum, abdomen.

etapes.justification: Both lengths must use the same unit: 12 cm = 120 mm.

sections.conclusion_markdown:
**Title:** Grasshopper, side view ($\times 3$).

The finished answer is a large, clean drawing with three regions, labels on ruled lines that do not cross, and a correct magnification. The legs and wings are attached to the thorax, and the hind legs are the longest because the grasshopper jumps.

items.erreur_markdown: Shading the drawing and colouring it with crayons so that it looks real.
items.pourquoi_faux: A biological drawing records structure. Shading and colour hide the outlines and earn no marks.
items.correction_markdown: Use only a sharp pencil and clear single lines.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing a small diagram in a corner of the answer space.
items.pourquoi_faux: When the question says 'large', a small drawing cannot show enough detail and loses the mark for size.
items.correction_markdown: Use most of the space available and leave room around the drawing for the labels.

items.erreur_markdown: Label lines that cross each other, stop short of the part, or end in the middle of the drawing without touching a structure.
items.pourquoi_faux: The examiner cannot tell which part you mean.
items.correction_markdown: Rule each line so that it ends exactly on the part, keep the lines from crossing, and write the labels horizontally.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing the legs and wings of an insect on the abdomen.
items.pourquoi_faux: In an insect, the legs and wings are attached to the thorax, so the drawing shows wrong structure.
items.correction_markdown: Place all three pairs of legs and the wings on the thorax.

items.erreur_markdown: Calculating the magnification as $\frac{\text{actual size}}{\text{size of drawing}}$, or dividing 12 cm by 40 mm without converting.
items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio is turned upside down, or two different units are mixed, so the result is wrong.
items.correction_markdown: Use $\frac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{actual size}}$ with both lengths in the same unit.

items.enonce_markdown: State five rules that a candidate should follow when making a biological drawing.
items.solution_markdown:
Award one mark for each correct rule, up to five:

1. Give the drawing a title.
2. Draw it large, using most of the space.
3. Use a sharp pencil and single continuous lines.
4. Do not shade or colour.
5. Keep the parts in correct proportion.
6. Label with ruled, horizontal labels whose lines touch the parts and do not cross.

**Any five of these rules earn full marks.**

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) A seed is 8 mm long. A student draws it 56 mm long. Calculate the magnification.

(b) An insect is drawn 45 mm long at a magnification of $\times 15$. Calculate the actual length of the insect.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{magnification} = \frac{56\ \text{mm}}{8\ \text{mm}} = 7$, so the magnification is $\times 7$.

(b) $\text{actual size} = \frac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{magnification}} = \frac{45\ \text{mm}}{15} = 3\ \text{mm}$.

**(a) $\times 7$; (b) 3 mm.**

items.enonce_markdown:
A student must draw the external features of a tilapia fish seen from the side.

(a) List eight features that should be labelled.

(b) The fish is 20 cm long and the drawing is 15 cm long. Calculate the magnification and say whether the drawing is enlarged or reduced.

(c) Give one reason why the student should not shade the scales.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Any eight of: mouth, nostril, eye, operculum, scales, lateral line, dorsal fin, pectoral fin, pelvic fin, anal fin, caudal fin.

(b) $\text{magnification} = \frac{15\ \text{cm}}{20\ \text{cm}} = 0.75$, written $\times 0.75$. The value is less than 1, so the drawing is **reduced**.

(c) Shading hides the outline of the structures and a biological drawing must show clear lines.

**Magnification $\times 0.75$, drawing reduced.**

items_markdown: A biological drawing is a clear, large, accurate record made with a sharp pencil, single lines, no shading and a title.
Labels are written horizontally on ruled lines that touch the part and never cross each other.
Magnification $= \frac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{actual size}}$, with both lengths in the same unit.
An insect has three regions (head, thorax, abdomen), with legs and wings attached to the thorax; a dipteran fly has one pair of wings and two halteres.
When a question says 'draw or describe', an ordered description naming each part and its position earns the same marks as a drawing.
